newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil markets gloomy over short-term prospects.
newsitem.headline: Brazil markets gloomy over short-term prospects.

text.p: Weak investor appetite for Brazil's much touted $750 million global bond is the latest in a spate of worrying financial news that has caused local markets to fret over the nation's medium-term economic prospects.
Market malaise over the past two weeks was triggered by September's surprisingly high $655 million trade gap.
Brazilian share prices on the Sao Paulo stock exchange have fallen 5.1 percent and the money market has been extremely volatile since the wide trade gap was announced on October 16.
"Up to about two weeks ago, the market had a very optimistic outlook. Then we got the trade numbers for September," a money market trader said.

Although Tuesday's release of larger-than-expected exports in October's fourth week eased some fears and caused a moderate rebound in stock prices, the trade picture remains the market's chief worry, traders said.
Their concern is that Brazil's demand for imported consumer and capital goods, spurred by a moderate economic recovery, might grow out of control and put too much pressure on the current account.

Such a scenario, the market fears, would force the government to slam on the brakes with higher interest rates and stiffer credit controls sometime early next year, which could throw the recuperating economy into recession.
Some traders say they fear the government could even resort to tinkering with exchange rate policy to reverse the deteriorating trade picture.
But economists say the market is overreacting to a set of serious, yet manageable problems.

"The market is more pessimistic and the worry it is creating is not realistic," said an economist at a leading U.S. bank in Brazil who asked not to be named. "The trade numbers are bad, but they will not prompt a change in monetary policy. There will not be a devaluation."

Still, the government's explanation that the large trade deficit was caused by a one-time boost in oil imports has not consoled market players, many of whom expect an October deficit of more than $1.0 billion.

Trade worries were cited as a key reason for the weak performance of Brazil's $750 million global bond launched on Monday in Asia, Europe and the United States. The five-year bond was priced at 265 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries and quickly widened by about 20 basis points in secondary trade.
Lukewarm reception of the bond helped push down Sao Paulo's Bovespa stock index 1.5 percent on Monday.

Also, ongoing concerns over the nation's fiscal woes were stoked this week by news reports that the National Treasury had found a 1.5 billion real shortfall in one of its accounts. The report raised fears that the government's job of unearthing Brazil's fiscal skeletons was far from over.

In addition to financial concerns, the market is worried about President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's bid to push through a constitutional amendment that would allow him to be re-elected and continue his economic reform drive.
The market wants Cardoso to have a second term, but is skeptical about the president's ability to push the plan through Congress.
Some traders, however, were optimistic about the market's prospects for a moderate recovery.

"There was a huge generation of buying ahead of the trade numbers and then we had a big downward revision. After a while we should see some strong buying because I don't think these worries are particularly significant," a debt trader said.
